entry.title: The Multi-Material Marbles Game: measuring real marbles to build an Ashby chart, open source for any classroom (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Students measure mechanical loss coefficient, thermal conductivity, electrical resistivity and density on marbles made from different material families, then plot their own Material Property Chart and reason about materials selection. Pilot studies report high engagement and increased interest in materials science; the CAD files, rules, material cards and equipment list are open source.

Why it matters here: A tactile route into structure-property relationships, the very topic the Wits study names as a learning barrier, and a ready-made open-source kit the CheMet team could trial alongside its own games.

Barnsdale, Daugela, Galos, Hülse, Tyler and Yu, 2025 ASEE Annual Conference and Exposition, Montreal; DOI 10.18260/1-2--56982 · Peer-reviewed conference paper, American Society for Engineering Education

entry.title: OU Analyse: weekly machine-learning risk scores for every distance student, and a decade of published evaluation (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
OU Analyse predicts each student's risk of failing the next assignment and updates the prediction weekly for tutors and student support teams, with the aim of improving retention across the Open University. The team has published on teachers' use and perceptions three years after implementation (LAK 2023), on co-creating an equality, diversity and inclusion dashboard to address awarding gaps (BJET 2024) and on a student-facing dashboard designed with students (LAK 2025, Journal of Learning Analytics 2025).

Why it matters here: A mature, evaluated system in a distance-learning setting close to much South African provision, with an open dataset the PASS models can be benchmarked against and a research track record on how teachers actually use predictions.

The Open University, OU Analyse (Knowledge Media Institute); Herodotou et al., Journal of Learning Analytics and LAK 2023 to 2025 · Institutional system with peer-reviewed evaluations

entry.title: Students write the questions, the faculty prints the board: a materials-science board game across three engineering degrees (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
A Party-and-Co style board game, its hexagonal board drawn from the graphene lattice, was built from more than 90 tests per category written by first-year mechanical engineering students and reviewed by staff, then played in Materials Science and Engineering (94 students), Microstructure and Phase Transformations (60) and Optical and Magnetic Behaviour of Materials (60). Between 80% and 84% of students said the game helped them understand the course, and 62% to 81% that they retained more than with their usual methods; participation ran at 80% to 86%.

Why it matters here: Closest published cousin of the CheMet study: a board game on phase transformations and microstructure, in the language of the students, with the survey-based evaluation the Wits team also plans. The students-as-authors step is worth borrowing for the co-design workshops.

Riquelme, de Prado, Bonache, Rams, Sánchez, Torres, Escalera Rodriguez, Rodrigo and Muñoz, Education Sciences 14(10), 1054 (2024), open access · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Materials Battleships and Materials Taboo: a gamified first-year materials course for more than 1,200 learners (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Two adapted board games, Materials Battleships and Materials Taboo, plus custom virtual emulators of material behaviour were run for over 1,200 first-year engineering learners in person and online. Surveys reported that gamification stimulated interest in materials science and the motivation to take part, with more students saying they would pursue materials courses later.

Why it matters here: Scale evidence for the Wits study: the same mix of table games and digital play the CheMet project proposes, tested on a large first-year cohort where retention of foundational concepts is the problem.

Earle, DiCecco, Binkley, Arshad, Lucentini, Tembrevilla and Yu, 2023 ASEE Annual Conference and Exposition · Peer-reviewed conference paper, American Society for Engineering Education

entry.title: Siyaphumelela: a national data-for-student-success network reaching 80% of South Africa's public university students (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Launched in 2014, Siyaphumelela works with post-school institutions to use data to improve access, retention, progression, graduation and work-readiness. It reports 20 partner universities, 80% of public university students reached, more than 1,500 university staff trained and R338 million invested, with an annual national conference and a focus on eliminating performance gaps by race, gender and socio-economic status.

Why it matters here: The South African ecosystem PASS sits inside: the institutions, staff and data practices already built through Siyaphumelela are the natural partners and audience for the Wits models and interventions, and the network's conference is a dissemination route.

Siyaphumelela, led by Saide in partnership with The Kresge Foundation (initiative site) · National initiative, funder-backed

entry.title: GPS Advising: more than 800 alerts, every undergraduate tracked daily, advisers who act the same week (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Georgia State runs predictive analytics over all undergraduates with a system of more than 800 alerts; when an alert fires, an adviser intervenes. The system went live in August 2012 and in one recent academic year generated more than 55,000 adviser-student meetings about specific alerts. Since 2012 first-year fall-to-spring retention has risen by five percentage points and graduating seniors take fewer excess courses.

Why it matters here: The best-known working model of what PASS proposes: prediction is only half the design; the other half is a person with time to act on each alert. Georgia State's alert-to-adviser loop is the pattern to test with Wits Business Intelligence Services and the School's advisers.

Georgia State University, Student Success Initiatives (institutional page) · Institutional programme page
